title: A Common Story
why: A subdued Italian drama about a couple left alone after their daughter moves out, holding on small gestures and stretches of silence; Anna Foglietta's 137-minute first feature, with Alba Rohrwacher

title: Arne Goes to Space
why: A quietly funny, tender oddity from rural Sweden: two aging brothers take in a small extraterrestrial whose ship crashes nearby, played straight and unhurried, with one brother's failing health running underneath.

title: Bedford Park
why: Forceful, unpolished first feature running 151 minutes, moving in English and Korean through inherited trauma and displacement as two people gradually grow close

title: Children Untold
why: Three hours of neorealism set in Tokyo after the war, tracking how conflict robs children of their youth, clear-eyed about kids left behind and mistreated, directed by a major Japanese filmmaker and featuring Koji Yakusho.

title: Head to Head
why: A Persian-language nested production whose comedy takes aim at how male filmmakers depict women and at state censorship, its ridicule sharpening as the political stakes grow heavier.

title: I Am Mario
why: Sharon Kleinberg's first feature from Mexico follows a trans taxi driver whose unexpected pregnancy backs him into a corner; a restrained, unhurried social drama, with transphobic slurs and graphic sex.

title: Idda
why: Slow, enigmatic study of two women whose strained bond surfaces during an ascent of Etna, with quiet menace, an unforeseen bereavement, and roaming, ominous camerawork; in Italian.

title: In Conversation With... Andrew Scott
why: An onstage interview with Andrew Scott covering the breadth of roles across his career; a nonfiction talk rather than a film with a story.

title: In Conversation With... Chris Rock
why: An in-person stage conversation with Chris Rock covering the many sides of his working life, presented as a comedy-inflected nonfiction event rather than a film with a story

title: Krux
why: Set in a village during WWII, Tony Vahl's 122-minute German-language first feature tracks ethical breakdown and mass panic through striking camerawork, and does not flinch from historical brutality.

title: Memories of a Forest
why: A hushed German-language drama set on the land, turning on what gets passed down and what is owed, and Katharina Rabl's first feature builds from terrain and withheld emotion more than from plot events.

title: Nosotros
why: Joaquin Ruano's first feature works in a subdued, precise register, following a rural Guatemalan man who moves to the city for work and finds a tender, precarious love with a trans woman while hostility presses in.

title: On Behalf of My Son
why: A 178-minute Brazilian drama on culpability and mourning, held at a quiet, controlled pitch, in which a mother travels to ask the bereaved families for forgiveness.

title: Seventeen
why: Naturalist drama unfolding across 17 hours as three queer Indigenous sex workers race personal deadlines in a rough part of central Vancouver; weighty and formally familiar, largely in English with some Cree.

title: Silenced Nights
why: A grim drama about drug-war shootings in Manila, filmed in vérité style on location in the Happyland slum, following an inquiry that runs into one dead end after another.

title: Sisters
why: A Spanish and Basque family drama about an assault within the family and the court case that follows, watchful in method and quietly grieving in tone, slow and weighty, subtitled, told in a familiar shape.

title: Strong Son
why: Ian Bawa's first feature follows a bodybuilder sunk in worry and self-doubt while looking after his father, breaking down in tears in public, set within a Sikh family; mostly English with some Punjabi.

title: The Daughters of Abraham
why: A first feature in French, played realistically, following a Muslim woman and a Jewish woman whose renewed friendship is upended by a sudden death; it looks hard at religion and gender but stays a close, small-scale drama.

title: The Fortunate Isles
why: Held-back epic about the remorse of conquest, shot with a hands-on camera and an ominous look all its own: a measured, poetic, formally heightened period piece on bondage and water scarcity, in Spanish and Arabic.

title: The World Before
why: A hushed adolescence story on a Korean island, its camera mostly fixed and watchful, drawing incident from ordinary life over 145 tender, faintly sorrowful minutes.

title: We Are Born Good
why: A funny, briskly paced comedy-drama about a quarrel that keeps ratcheting up, following Hong Kong characters buried in debt whom grief, rage and fatigue have already ground down

title: What Lies Between Us
why: A Danish drama, unsettling and tense, in which mothers face an allegation of sexual assault; its storytelling is straightforward, its rhythm well controlled, its themes hard, its acting forceful.

title: Wild Wild East
why: Part western, part wartime noir, Jan Holoubek's tense film unfolds in occupied Poland in 1943, tracing greed and treachery among shell-shocked villagers and Nazi officials; 135 minutes, in Polish, German and Ukrainian.

title: Zjili: A Story of Sisterhood and The Burdens of Excess
why: A Ghanaian social-realist film about kayayei head porters, handled plainly rather than for shock value, running 149 minutes in Dagbani and Twi, built on research and dedicated to a woman killed by a load she was carrying.

title: A Girl Unknown
why: Told in chapters over 158 minutes and in Chinese, it follows a girl through abandonment and repeated uprooting, played with held-back performances, subdued and sore but not without hope.

title: After Elena
why: A Spanish-language drama about a family after a death that stays soft-edged and refuses to judge or turn maudlin, drawing its weight from tiny gestures, comic absurdity and melancholy.

title: Ah Girl
why: Ang's own childhood feeds this drama set in 1990s Singapore, where gentle camerawork, everyday texture and blurred dream passages carry a girl through her parents' split with a sweet-sour sense of already-lived memory.

title: Ashes
why: An immigrant story in Spanish and Catalan about being uprooted repeatedly and enduring the hardest ordeals, handled with adult restraint and shading, told in familiar form and weighted with emotional cost

title: Babies
why: A crowd-pleasing ensemble comedy with a big cast, weighing the choice of parenthood; warm, familiar in shape, funny and down-to-earth without much riding on it.

title: Ben'Imana
why: Set in Rwanda's gacaca tribunals, this Kinyarwanda-language film deals with genocide trauma and mothers bearing their rapists' children, building a story across generations; it took the Camera d'Or and runs 131 minutes.

title: Congo Boy
why: Shot with a restless handheld camera and cut to the beat of the hero's rapping, this Sango, French and Lingala film follows a scrambling teenage refugee through hard circumstances with warmth and lift rather than despair

title: Eklipse
why: A lyrically realist story of growing up in the Austrian countryside in 1999, in German, mixing home-video tape into the fiction, with the concealed truth of a father's sickness giving it a subdued weight.

title: Elephants in the Fog
why: Abinash Bikram Shah's first feature pairs toughness with gentleness, casting non-professionals and filming the green Nepali landscape in fine detail, as a Kinnar community's old rules press against modern desires.

title: Evil Genius
why: A dramatized true-crime case staged with the sly comic menace of a Coen Brothers picture, full of killings and double-crosses, carried by a Gala-scale cast and a plot that doubles back in time.

title: Four Seasons in Java
why: Andini's largest-scale work to date, a 167-minute drama centred on a woman confronting sexual violence, mixing fantastical elements with striking imagery and layered metaphor; heavy going and dark.

title: Furies
why: Set against Lebanon's frozen banking system, this 164-minute Arabic-language robbery thriller in Beirut runs on quick cutting and a tense countdown as its characters chase time they cannot afford to lose.

title: Future Tense
why: Jenna Cato Bass directs a time-travel science fiction picture, spoken partly in Xhosa and Afrikaans, that binds a love story to fears of climate breakdown and the brutality of the colonial era.

title: Girl Group
why: A broadly appealing music comedy stacked with comic performers and a strong song selection, running a familiar redemption path as a washed-up pop singer mentors aspiring young performers.

title: God Bless You, Mr Kopu
why: Alex Liu's debut cuts satire against the strut of 1970s hustler and action pictures, accelerating into a fast, tense thriller: a dark comedy played largely in English but rooted in specific Tongan life.

title: Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!
why: A Tokyo grief story built as a mannered mix of melodrama and daydream: odd, light-footed, playful, with imagined detours including a giant crow and Dirty Dancing; mostly in Japanese and Spanish, 151 min.

title: Iron Boy
why: An autobiographical coming-of-age tale in French, animated in hand-painted images by a director who once worked at Pixar, lovely and playful in tone, and honoured by a special jury award at Cannes

title: Ken Russell's The Devils
why: Russell's delirious, boundary-breaking film treats the Loudun hysteria, torture and exorcism at once as history, horror film and political allegory, in saturated baroque style with strong body-horror content.

title: Kissed
why: Carries the same otherworldly air as Crash and Exotica: a hazy, trance-bound drama about necrophilia that holds the real and the imagined in equilibrium instead of tipping into horror.

title: L'AUTRE
why: Alexandre Franchi's black-humoured thriller keeps a man's endangered mind and body inside one hospital room, running on medicated unreality, physical immediacy, stretches of dread, and restless nerve.

title: La Gradiva
why: Running 175 minutes, this French-Italian ensemble film about young people growing up, set in Pompeii, pairs lyrical imagery with serious ideas and a shooting style close to documentary.

title: Light Pillar
why: A sad, boldly designed film about loneliness that draws the waking world by hand and shoots the VR world live, unhurried and rueful, taking real formal risks while pulling you in gently.

title: Long Long Night
why: Glowing animated fable pairing a rhino with a penguin, swinging between comedy and deep grief amid poachers and death; a Korean-language first feature in the Centrepiece slot.

title: Love is the monster
why: A daring dystopia set in the tropics, part kidnapping thriller and part genre exercise, building dread around class division, with Paulina Garcia leading a Spanish-language cast.

title: Muyi
why: A French-language animated fable about growing up, set in China, whose appeal rests on inventive design and playful figures such as a tiger that eats no meat and a guide with magic.

title: Onwards and Sideways
why: A familiar British sickness comedy-drama mixing grief, jokes, and slowly earned intimacy; it treats degenerative illness plainly while letting cheeky humour lighten it, running an easy 140 minutes suited to a Gala slot

title: Our Loves
why: A 147-minute film in Hebrew and Arabic built from linked storylines, each carrying its own private sorrow, until disaster pushes the characters into collective survival; its power lies in feeling and depth rather than momentum.

title: Pretenders
why: A standard-format music documentary built from interviews and archive footage about Chrissie Hynde, hard-edged and sharply dressed, with exciting live clips and a death shaping its middle section.

title: Soumsoum, The Night of the Stars
why: Set on Chad's Ennedi plateau, Haroun follows a girl shunned for her second sight, grounding fantasy in realism; slow and myth-inflected, spoken in Arabic and French, weighted toward banishment and the dead

title: The Difficult Bride
why: A Bengali-language Centrepiece drama with a body-horror edge, full of vivid visions of catfish, snakes and movement beneath the skin, more concerned with the suffocating demands placed on a bride than with narrative drive.

title: The Dreamed Adventure
why: Grisebach's 194-minute film in Bulgarian, awarded the Jury Prize at Cannes, builds slowly and with great control around diesel smuggling and buried memory, where the crime story is only a small trace of something larger and hazier

title: The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd
why: An Oklahoma-set drama inside a maximum security prison, 151 minutes tracing an abusive marriage, guilt, and punishment; familiar in shape and weighty in tone, carried by its lead actors.

title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
why: A quiet crime story that doubles as a reflection on a shifting era, made in the character-focused style of 1970s New Hollywood, with Turturro's appeal holding it together.

title: The Violinist
why: Animated love story set against WWII Singapore, following its two musicians across eighty years through grief, memory and endurance; runs 144 minutes and took the Cristal, Annecy's top feature award.

title: The bovine with the curved horns
why: A boy's perspective on paramilitary violence in the Ciénaga Grande, told through Caribbean fantasy and magical realism, acted by locals, blending folklore with everyday rhythm in finely graded black-and-white.

title: Toy Gun Bandit
why: A high-octane crime comedy from Quebec whose chaos keeps mounting, driven by jittery, heedless momentum and offset by real tenderness plus a storyline about a young addict sliding downward.

title: Up Against It
why: A sharp-edged comedy that reworks screwball conventions around a daughter's leukemia diagnosis, carried by its name cast in a 152-minute Gala slot.

title: We Are All Strangers
why: Running 187 minutes, Anthony Chen ends his Growing Up trilogy with an unhurried, humane portrait of a makeshift family, its aches and maturing, and the class rifts around them, mostly spoken in Mandarin

title: Where the River Begins
why: Naturalistic, rough-edged drama about migration cast with non-professional Indigenous performers, dealing with displacement and paramilitary violence, though pitched more lyrically and tenderly than a tense thriller

title: Ancestors
why: A hypnotic drift through 1980s London rendered like a half-remembered dream, where recollection and yearning blur; a slow, vision-filled lament for what the AIDS years left behind, sorrowful yet never sinking into hopelessness.

title: Magazine
why: A dialogue-driven, watchful first feature following a young poet interning in the literary world before #MeToo; the storytelling is traditional and the social observation sharp, running a fairly long 135 minutes.

title: Masc
why: Bertil Nilsson's first feature, filmed across a year in five parts, watches a young gay neurodivergent man adjust himself across London settings, avoiding crisis or coming-out beats, and closing on a wordless surprise.

title: Purgatory
why: Set in the 1980s, a warm and lightly comic growing-up story that sits alongside Lady Bird and Eighth Grade, told in familiar form and running 134 minutes

title: Salvation
why: Confident first feature from Scotland following a self-deluding aspiring life coach: a social-realist portrait that is uncomfortable to watch and quietly unsettling, funny in places yet earnest and driven by desperation.

title: Voices
why: A 1967 Detroit story confined to one motel room, dark in the manner of crime cinema and centred on a scam born of desperation, its catchy song sequences opening up the grim tale of fame's corruption.

title: Back in Black
why: Sharp-toothed dark comedy: Walken is a foul-tongued mortician whose granddaughter engineers deadly accidents to bring business to the family funeral parlour, told plainly with big laughs and only a light macabre streak

title: How We Stand
why: A gripping story of three sisters whose lives bear the mark of Indigenous relocation programs, carrying trauma and sexual violence yet buoyed by magic-realist touches and comic jabs at the Hollywood western

title: Lemonade
why: Kim Bartley's first fiction feature follows a young man aging out of Irish foster care, watching him closely for humour, affection and small everyday pleasures instead of bleakness, with Barry Keoghan steadying the film.

title: Neverman
why: A trans elder losing her memory to Alzheimer's is kept in a chilly, forbidding care facility, her past surfacing in flashback; the result is a weighty, mostly familiar drama with a slight undercurrent of menace.

title: Smudge the Blades
why: An underdog hockey comedy-drama following the Bad News Bears template, tougher and heavier in tone, with fast-paced on-ice action and jokes, unfolding on a reserve in Northern Alberta.

title: Sunburn
why: Relaxed, comic teen hangout picture in a Dazed and Confused vein, hot and colour-drenched onscreen, though it moves without much plot and keeps the stakes small.

title: Tangles
why: Leah Nelson adapts Sarah Leavitt's Alzheimer's memoir in hand-drawn 2D animation, an emotionally weighty story lightened by a voice cast stacked with comedians

title: The Betrayers
why: Absorbing, polished adaptation of a novel: a moral and political drama set in Yalta, mostly in English yet saturated in Soviet-Israeli history, driven by talk and character instead of momentum.

title: The Surgeon
why: Michelle Yeoh anchors a fast, brutal action picture built on tight fight choreography, surgical gore and well-chosen rock cuts, working squarely inside blockbuster genre form.

title: Trash Mountain
why: A witty, perceptive film about returning home, mixing disrespectful humour with warmth; familiar indie dramedy shape, but with genuine mourning running beneath it.

title: Alice
why: A large-scale French-language costume drama about Alice Guy-Blache in Belle Epoque Paris, starring Berenice Bejo, told in a familiar prestige-biopic mode.

title: Blindspot Berlin
why: A gripping police-investigation drama that pieces together the run-up to the 2016 Breitscheidplatz attack, holding nothing back as it digs into wiretaps, informants and radicalization, in German, Arabic and Turkish.

title: Oxygen Masks Will (Not) Drop Automatically
why: Set in 1980s Brazil, this Portuguese-language drama runs 140 minutes and tells a conventional story of the AIDS years, its bright nightclub world running alongside shame and mortality, pleasure and fear inseparable

title: YAGA
why: A coastal-town investigation shaded by the Baba Yaga legend, mixing scares with mystery-solving, dry back-and-forth between its leads, and a persistent sense that something inhuman waits just out of sight

title: American Hostage
why: A true-story siege thriller centred on broadcast ethics and the blurred line between reporting an event and becoming part of it, a fairly standard Primetime series whose tension comes from talk and procedure.

title: Below
why: A Newfoundland family story crossed with something monstrous in the water, told in familiar creature-feature shape, holding domestic warmth against cold sea horror.

title: Crystal Lake
why: An A24-produced Friday the 13th prequel series that traces Pamela Voorhees through her grief after Jason's drowning while piling up the bodies and delivering gory fun.

title: Slow Horses
why: Episodes of a spy series that keeps up its driving pace and grim comedy, with sharp writing that makes the unglamorous business of espionage consistently fun to watch

title: The Diary of a Chambermaid
why: Placed in Wavelengths as Jude's broadly comic attack on present-day servitude: a French/Romanian satire heavy on dialogue and formal risk, yet warmer toward its heroine than expected.

title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
why: Harlem Renaissance figures gathered at a 1972 party, filmed with several 16mm cameras and left loose and talk-driven, the exchanges by turns funny, impassioned, and touched with sadness, preserving that movement as it lived

title: Growth of the Soil
why: Running 185 minutes, this straightforwardly told period epic follows the hardships of carving out a farm in northern Norway, staged in a strictly realist register and performed with weight and restraint.

title: Making Waves With... Hudson Williams
why: This is a live discussion with actor Hudson Williams programmed under TIFF Next Wave rather than a screening, so it takes the shape of an on-stage interview and has no film form to speak of.

title: Pelechian Project
why: Speechless nonfiction built from montage, dense in image and score, moving between exhilaration and grief, each film a bruising tribute to human life and its cycles; radical in form, presented in new restorations.

title: In Conversation With... Lee Min-ho
why: An in-person stage interview with Lee Min-ho, a figure central to Korean pop culture worldwide; it screens nothing, sitting nearest to nonfiction discussion rooted in Korean-language cultural background.

screenings.v: VISA Screening Room at the Princess of Wales Theatre
screenings.r: VISA Screening Room at the Princess of Wales Theatre

title: In Conversation With... Rachel Morrison
why: An in-person stage discussion with Rachel Morrison, nominated for an Oscar as a cinematographer and now directing, tracing her career path: nonfiction talk rather than a screening, centred on craft, not on drama or genre.

title: At Night
why: Beatrice Gibson's first feature in Wavelengths, shot on 16mm, works as collective autofiction in a poetic register rather than conventional storytelling, sliding among fiction, documentary, and dream in several languages, with a sombre mood

title: Double Freedom
why: In Wavelengths, Alonso answers his own La libertad with an unhurried 35mm portrait of daily labour, cast with non-actors, that turns away from conventional storytelling and thinks patiently about caretaking and what freedom means.

title: Everything Else is Noise
why: Wavelengths hosts Pereda's wry, self-aware social comedy of small disasters, built as a chamber piece with pared-down means and a Lubitsch-like lightness, running 101 minutes in Spanish

title: Life of Jorge Luis Borges
why: Running 370 minutes in Wavelengths, Llinas, who made La Flor, builds an essay film that keeps fact and fabrication indistinguishable: learned, wandering, full of play, and asking a great deal of its audience

title: London
why: A 150-minute German-language avant-garde road film built from stationary in-car talk, filmed with old-style rear projection, drawing on James Benning, its passengers trading existential talk with the driver.

title: My Wife Cries
why: A German-language work of slow, contemplative art cinema: Schanelec shoots on 35mm in a grave, stripped-down key, building a lament of estrangement and hurt from framings like still-life paintings, broken by odd interruptions.

title: Nobody's Violence
why: Wavelengths hosts Cote's dystopian film about a euthanasia facilitator, 148 minutes in French, which keeps changing form from science-fiction fable to conspiracy thriller to comedy in Bunuel's vein, driven throughout by an unsettled energy

title: REDEFINED | Short Film Showcase
why: A set of five shorts by Indigenous and Canadian directors working in a first-person mode, taking up questions of heritage, identity, where one belongs and sovereignty, with a form that leans essayistic and documentary.

title: Short Cuts 2026 / Strange Cuts
why: The programme note offered nothing specific, so the placement rests on the title Strange Cuts alone, which points to shorts with genre leanings and unconventional form drawn from a range of sources.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 01
why: The source text is only TIFF's generic organizational blurb and says nothing about the films, so the slot rests on standard Short Cuts expectations: a varied shorts block with some experimental technique and entries from abroad.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 02
why: Note is only TIFF's boilerplate mission statement, so placement rests entirely on the Short Cuts prior: a mixed 131-min shorts block of varied tone and language.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 03
why: The source text is only TIFF's standard mission blurb and says nothing about the films, so the placement defaults to typical Short Cuts patterns: a mix of forms, a few titles with subtitles, and a compilation spanning different tones.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 04
why: The programmer text is just TIFF's standard institutional mission language and says nothing about the films, so this 130-minute mixed-form shorts collection sits at the default Short Cuts values.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 05
why: Note is boilerplate mission text with no film detail; placements default to Short Cuts shorts-programme averages of mixed tone and moderate formal play.

title: Short Cuts 2026 Programme 06
why: Note is boilerplate mission statement with no film detail; placed at neutral defaults for a mixed Short Cuts anthology programme, which tends toward mild formal play and varied language.

title: The Black Box is Orange
why: Yuula Benivolski's self-portrait essay work unfolds across ten formally varied sections, using hand-developed 16mm and sound set against image to confront the 1948 Nakba, occupation, and her own implicated recollections.

title: The Remotes
why: A 183-minute Wavelengths entry in Tagalog that runs long and skips between scenes, mixing science fiction, noir and detective work with trance-like nocturnal driving and the sorrow left by colonial history.

title: Wavelengths 1: House and Home
why: A Wavelengths shorts set of sensory, poem-like essay works about dwelling and remembrance, ranging from archive-based reflection to a calmly furious account of housing and exploitation.

title: Wavelengths 2: This Suffocating Now
why: A Wavelengths shorts set built on essayistic work and camera-made effects: Tafakory's clear, multi-strand history, Kosugi's poetic 8mm, a walk shot on night vision, and a blunt, physical political charge

title: Wavelengths 3: Time and Tide
why: A Wavelengths short-film selection spanning 65mm formal experiment, Baroque trompe l'oeil, salvaged 8mm footage of Roma migration, and an essay drawing on Duras and Conrad: openly avant-garde, meditative work.

title: Wavelengths: Anoushahpour/Aljafari
why: A Wavelengths double bill of slow, essayistic nonfiction about recollection and invention: Anoushahpour's portrait of Kurdish villages built around wedding embroideries, and Aljafari's quiet observation of Masao Adachi seeking a passport.
